name: Humming exercises

lead: Humming exercises involve producing a sustained tone with the lips closed, so sound resonates in the head and throat and passes through the nose. In voice-improvement discussions it is mentioned as a gentle warm-up before speaking or singing.
The sources reviewed describe humming in general terms and do not cover it as a vocal warm-up; no studies on humming specifically as an appearance or voice-attractiveness practice were found.

paras: A hum is made with the mouth closed, so the tone resonates in the nasal and throat passages. Practitioners describe the closed-mouth position as a low-effort way to begin phonating.

No specific risks are documented in the sources reviewed. Voice clinicians generally advise that any vocal practice that causes pain or hoarseness be stopped, which is general guidance rather than a finding about humming.

lead: A hum is a wordless tone produced with the mouth closed, so the sound passes through the nose.[1] In looksmaxxing and voice-improvement discussions, humming exercises are described as a vocal warm-up: a way to start phonation gently before speaking or singing.

The reference material on humming consists of general descriptions of the sound and its cultural and evolutionary interpretations; it does not examine humming as a voice-training technique. No studies were found testing humming exercises for changing perceived vocal attractiveness or authority.

paras: Humming is described as a monotone or lightly varying tone made with closed lips, with air resonating in the passages of the head and throat.[1] It is also a feature of music, with melodies sometimes hummed rather than sung.[1]

Humming is mentioned in voice-improvement discussions as a warm-up alongside other vocal exercises. Related semi-occluded exercises, such as phonating through a straw, have a larger published literature in voice science.
